section_title: How does God sustain David when every hiding place seems unsafe?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 7 When Saul was told that David had gone to Keilah, he said, “God has delivered him into my hand, for he has trapped himself by entering a town with gates and bars.” 8 Then Saul summoned all his troops to go to war at Keilah and besiege David and his men. 9 When David learned that Saul was plotting evil against him, he said to Abiathar the priest, “Bring the ephod.” 10 And David said, “O LORD, God of Israel, Your servant has heard that Saul intends to come to Keilah and destroy the city on my account. 11 Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me into his hand? Will Saul come down, as Your servant has heard? O LORD, God of Israel, please tell Your servant.” “He will,” said the LORD. 12 So David asked, “Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me and my men into the hand of Saul?” “They will,” said the LORD. 13 Then David and his men, about six hundred strong, set out and departed from Keilah, moving from place to place. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he declined to go forth. 14 And David stayed in the wilderness strongholds and in the hill country of the Wilderness of Ziph. Day after day Saul searched for him, but God would not deliver David into his hand.

15 While David was in Horesh in the Wilderness of Ziph, he saw that Saul had come out to take his life. 16 And Saul’s son Jonathan came to David in Horesh and strengthened his hand in God, 17 saying, “Do not be afraid, for my father Saul will never lay a hand on you. And you will be king over Israel, and I will be your second-in-command. Even my father Saul knows this is true.” 18 So the two of them made a covenant before the LORD. And David remained in Horesh, while Jonathan went home.

19 Then the Ziphites came up to Saul at Gibeah and said, “Is not David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah south of Jeshimon? 20 Now, O king, come down whenever your soul desires, and we will be responsible for delivering him into your hand.” 21 “May you be blessed by the LORD,” replied Saul, “for you have had compassion on me. 22 Please go and prepare further. Investigate and watch carefully where he goes and who has seen him there, for I am told that he is extremely cunning. 23 Observe and find out all the places where he hides. Then come back to me with certainty, and I will go with you. If he is in the land, I will search him out among all the clans of Judah.”

24 So they set out and went to Ziph ahead of Saul. Now David and his men were in the Wilderness of Maon in the Arabah south of Jeshimon, 25 and Saul and his men went to seek him. When David was told about it, he went down to the rock and stayed in the Wilderness of Maon. And when Saul heard of this, he pursued David there. 26 Saul was proceeding along one side of the mountain, and David and his men along the other side. Even though David was hurrying to get away, Saul and his men were closing in on David and his men to capture them. 27 Then a messenger came to Saul, saying, “Come quickly, for the Philistines have raided the land!” 28 So Saul broke off his pursuit of David and went to meet the Philistines. That is why that place is called Sela-hammahlekoth. 29 And David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of En-gedi.

context_lines: Saul hears that David has entered Keilah and thinks its gates and bars will trap him. He claims God has handed David over. David instead asks the LORD what will happen: will Saul come, and will the citizens surrender him? On receiving the warning that they will, David leaves with about six hundred men. Saul then abandons the planned siege.

The pursuit continues in the wilderness. Jonathan comes to Horesh and strengthens David in God, affirming that David will become king. He hopes to serve as David’s second-in-command, and they make a covenant before the LORD. Jonathan then returns home while David remains in hiding.

The Ziphites report David’s whereabouts to Saul and offer to hand him over. Saul blesses them for their concern for him and demands detailed information about the hiding places. He pursues David into the Wilderness of Maon, where the two groups move on opposite sides of a mountain and Saul closes in.

At that moment a messenger reports a Philistine raid. Saul breaks off the pursuit to meet the attackers, and David moves to the strongholds of En-gedi. The escape brings the chapter’s earlier statement into focus: Saul searches day after day, but God does not deliver David into his hand.
The heading of [Psalm 54](https://biblehub.com/bsb/psalms/54.htm) identifies the Ziphites’ report to Saul. Its plea for rescue and confidence in God as helper give words to faith under this threat.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/), [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/23.htm) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/23.htm) read the answers at Keilah as describing what would happen if David stayed. His departure changes the circumstances. The warning guides him into action; it is not a prediction that he must remain and be captured.

[Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/23.htm) sees Jonathan’s encouragement as friendship directing David toward God. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) reads his expectation of a second place as willingness to accept David’s kingship. Jonathan’s hope for his own role is not fulfilled: [1 Samuel 31:1–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_samuel/31.htm) later records his death before David takes the throne.

[Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/23.htm) understand the covenant here as a renewal of their friendship. The passage does not give new terms for a government appointment. Its emphasis is their commitment before the LORD in a time of danger.

[Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/23.htm) contrasts Saul’s religious language with his pursuit of David. Calling the informers blessed does not prove God approves the pursuit. Henry and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/23.htm) also see God’s care in the messenger arriving just as David is being surrounded. The needed escape comes through an interruption Saul has to answer.
god_plan_lines: God’s sustaining care reaches David through both encouragement and a way of escape. Jonathan cannot remove the danger, but he helps David remember the future God has opened. The later interruption preserves David when human arrangements appear to be closing around him.

For Christ’s people, [Hebrews 10:19–25](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/10.htm) joins confidence in God with the work of encouraging one another. Jesus opens the way into God’s presence, God’s faithfulness gives reason to hold firmly to hope, and believers are to spur one another toward love and good deeds.

This is a shared theme of faith sustained in community, rather than a promise that every threatened believer will escape as David did. God’s purpose includes people helping one another keep trusting Him while the outcome is still unseen.
